speaker: Tano Santos
text: I think what you said, Li Lu, about this combination of being extraordinary, dangerous, and our not completely understanding why it is generating some of the answers it is generating, would require a human in the loop to check over it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Right.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Once again, it’s going to be the scarce supply of this skill, of the person monitoring the artificial intelligence output, that will determine where rents are going to be located.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That’s right.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: That effectively means if you’re smart and can communicate effectively with that AI inside any domain, you’re going to be the scarce resource, and probably the rents are going to accrue to you.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Do I understand this correctly?

speaker: Li Lu
text: I think that’s somewhere along those lines.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It has different aspects and nuances, but I think that’s the case in the end.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Let’s start projecting these ideas.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: One of the things that is most striking when we walk into the classroom—there are many of my colleagues here teaching capital markets, financial markets, value investing, investing in general—is that this is one peculiar market.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I have a very vague question for you.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: The market seems to be driven by a very low number of companies that are pushing the technological frontier.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: The world seems dependent on these companies to push this frontier, and as a result, valuations are completely distorted by that.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: There’s a plot I show my students: the market capitalization of the company with the highest market capitalization, normalized by GDP.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: That number traditionally has been between 2 and 4 percent.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: It is now about 15 percent with Nvidia.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: How do you think about this market, one that is becoming overly dependent on those few companies, with a very high beta to those companies?

speaker: Tano Santos
text: How do we design portfolios to protect ourselves against the shocks of this technology?

speaker: Li Lu
text: The market always does peculiar things.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Yes.

speaker: Li Lu
text: From the very beginning, we go through this, and we’ll probably continue to do so.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You don’t have to be dictated to by what the market decides to do at any given time.

speaker: Li Lu
text: This is one of the most important insights and contributions from Ben Graham himself.

speaker: Li Lu
text: At this point, if you look at the proposition of one recent prospectus that I read.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Here’s a company that calls itself a research lab, yet it burns through tens of billions and promises to continue burning through hundreds of billions of dollars.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It promises a transformative technology, but at the same time has a 10 percent chance of killing everyone.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It wrote that in the prospectus and invited everybody to put in at least $100 billion at a $2 trillion valuation.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If there is there any inconsistency or irony?!

speaker: Li Lu
text: Then this is.

speaker: Li Lu
text: This is one extreme illustration of how irrational the market gets.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It cannot both be true, but that’s where they are.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It also tells you that things are not rational and not sustainable.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Eventually, they won’t continue.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Those are also the rules of the market, if you look throughout the centuries.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They do strange things over a long period of time.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Take the S&P since 2010, for example.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the last 16 years, it averaged 14 or 15 percent.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the preceding 10 years, from 2000 to 2010, it averaged exactly zero — in fact, slightly negative for 10 years.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you average the last 26 years, you get high single digits, and that is roughly right over the long term.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If GDP grew in that period maybe 2 percent, and you have 2 to 3 percent inflation, you average about 4 to 5 percent nominal growth.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Publicly listed companies do slightly better, especially those chosen by elimination to be the 500 best companies.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You come up with high single digits, and that is where the long-term average has been.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That should serve as a basic grounding pillar of getting what you deserve and how the market rationalizes over a longer period.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But it is punctuated by periods, sometimes long periods, when it goes to extremes.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The example we just cited does strike people as, at a minimum, odd.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That happens throughout history.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If we ground society in the sense that a super-creature is simply not allowed or tolerated, it won’t go there.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If it stays in the realm of tools, it will be like any other tool, with costs and benefits associated with it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Therefore, financial discipline and capital market discipline will eventually apply.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The way you get there is through multiple ups and downs and boom and bust cycles, and that’s also fine.

speaker: Li Lu
text: From that perspective, the bifurcation as a result of it — at any given time, you don’t create an enormous amount of new capital.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If it is overwhelmingly driven to the top, that means you also have a whole bunch of otherwise wonderful businesses trading at very low prices.

speaker: Li Lu
text: This is the same here, in China, or anywhere else.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In China, it is probably more extreme, as some of the Chinese participants would be well aware.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Over time, the weight of the market will dictate the long-term returns of investors.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You still get what you deserve in the end.

speaker: Li Lu
text: There’s not much of a free lunch, even if it appears to be for a period of time, even a long period.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Over the longer term, it will be weighed out by the natural weight of market rationalization itself.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That’s why it has existed for a few hundred years already.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I would say this bifurcation offers those with a rational mind a better opportunity set than at other times, if you stay rational, which is very difficult.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It’s easy to get swept up, especially when you have a big technology wave.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Your margin of imagination can expand dramatically.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The speculative side of the market gets much more active, and the imagination becomes wilder, so the exaggerations tend to be more extreme.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But for a rational mind, those create a better long-term opportunity set than otherwise.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: You mentioned China briefly there.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Let’s talk a little bit about that.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I just came back from China.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I was teaching the participants in Hong Kong, and I took advantage of that occasion to do a couple of cases on Chinese companies and study the Chinese market a little.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: It’s been quite a ride over the last few years.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: How do you think about the Chinese market these days, with the problems in the Chinese economy associated with the real estate bust and the banking crisis?

speaker: Tano Santos
text: It looks reminiscent of some of the things we’ve seen in other places.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: How do you see investing in China these days?

speaker: Li Lu
text: You mentioned the Chinese market.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you look at the last 10 years, it has basically been stagnant.

speaker: Li Lu
text: What happened in those 10 years is fascinating.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Ten years ago, the Chinese government had a decision to make.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They had achieved somewhat of a middle-income level.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The question was: How do we break away from it?

speaker: Li Lu
text: So many countries have reached that level and stagnated there, so much so that there is a term to describe it – the middle-income trap.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Dozens of countries achieved that and stayed there 40 or 50 years later.

speaker: Li Lu
text: China is a large economy, so the question naturally is: What keeps a middle-income country stagnant and prevents it from breaking through the ceiling?

speaker: Li Lu
text: You manufacture, you industrialize, you go with mid- to low-end manufacturing, but never break away from it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They had a decision to make.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Do we want to break out, and can we do something to accelerate that process or make sure it happens?

speaker: Li Lu
text: On its natural course, a lot of countries have failed to achieve that and stayed there for 40 or 50 years, some countries even longer.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They embarked on this process of deliberately migrating the economy from low- to mid-end manufacturing into mid- to high-end manufacturing.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Instead of a five-year plan, they had a 10- year plan called Made in China 2025, in which they listed about 10 major objectives aimed at transforming Chinese basic manufacturing from low- to mid-end into mid- to high-end.

speaker: Li Lu
text: A few years after that started, the first Trump administration came on board and started the trade war.

speaker: Li Lu
text: This reinforced their idea that not only might they not break through that ceiling on their own natural course, but other countries might deliberately constrain them underneath it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The first Trump administration was followed by the Biden administration, which not only kept the trade tariffs but also added more technology restrictions.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Five years into the 10-year plan, by 2021, the Chinese government doubled down on that direction.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In addition to migrating manufacturing into the mid- to high-end, it added technological self- sufficiency, particularly in areas where they had real bottlenecks: semiconductors, big aircraft engines, operating software code, and so on.

speaker: Li Lu
text: There was a long list China was facing.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That started another five years of doubling down and accelerating that process.

speaker: Li Lu
text: When you try to achieve those impossible goals that so many countries have failed to achieve, it doesn’t come without deep and heavy costs.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That has been the model by which China developed its economy.

speaker: Li Lu
text: At different periods, they have big objectives and targets, with big costs associated with them.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You mentioned real estate.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the last five years, one of the principal costs of achieving that goal has been the balance sheets and family wealth of middle-class Chinese families.

speaker: Li Lu
text: By 2021, real estate prices reached their peak.

speaker: Li Lu
text: A typical middle-class Chinese family had 70 percent of its net worth tied up in the home it owned.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But that home carried roughly 50 percent leverage through a mortgage.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the next five years, until now, real estate prices nationwide lost about 40 percent of their value on average.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They saw their entire family fortune go down 60 to 70 percent on average.

speaker: Li Lu
text: When that happens, what do you do?
